title: What expenses are excluded from R&D tax credits?
description: The R&D tax credit excludes costs outside IRC § 41(b) or tied to § 41(d)(4) activities, such as overhead, fringe benefits and foreign research.
summary: Under U.S. federal law, the R&D tax credit excludes expenses that fall outside the qualified research expense categories of IRC § 41(b) or relate to activities barred by § 41(d)(4). Excluded costs include research after commercial production, overhead and G&A, fringe benefits, depreciable property, funded research, and foreign research, so businesses must segregate them to avoid audit disallowances.

body.text: Under U.S. federal law, the R&D tax credit excludes expenses that fall outside the qualified research expense categories of IRC § 41(b) or relate to activities barred by § 41(d)(4). Excluded costs include research after commercial production, overhead and G&A, fringe benefits, depreciable property, funded research, and foreign research, so businesses must segregate them to avoid audit disallowances.
1. Why exclusions matter

In United States federal tax administration, the statutory boundary between qualifying and excluded expenses operates on two distinct levels. First, at the activity level, IRC § 41(d)(1) establishes the affirmative four-part threshold for "qualified research," while IRC § 41(d)(4) enumerates eight categorical activity exclusions that disqualify all associated costs even if the underlying project might otherwise appear technical in nature. Second, at the expenditure level, IRC § 41(b) strictly confines QREs to three exhaustive cost categories—in-house wages for qualified services, supplies used in the conduct of qualified research, and specified computer rental or contract research payments—thereby excluding overhead, general and administrative expenses, fringe benefits, capital equipment, and real property by omission as well as by explicit regulatory rule under Treas. Reg. § 1.41-2.
2. The U.S. baseline: what "qualified research" requires

Excluded expenses in the United States R&D tax credit regime are fundamentally defined as any expenditure that either fails to fit within the exhaustive QRE categories of IRC § 41(b) or relates to an activity falling outside the statutory definition of "qualified research" under IRC § 41(d). Under IRC § 41(d)(1), as currently in force, research constitutes "qualified research" only if all four statutory requirements are satisfied concurrently for each discrete business component:

items: Section 174A Domestic Research Expense Test (§ 41(d)(1)(A)): The expenditures with respect to the research must be eligible to be treated as domestic research or experimental expenditures under IRC § 174A (meaning costs incurred in the experimental or laboratory sense to eliminate uncertainty concerning the development or improvement of a product, process, formula, invention, pilot model, or technique under Treas. Reg. § 1.174-2(a)(1)).

Technological in Nature Test (§ 41(d)(1)(B)(i)): The research must be undertaken for the purpose of discovering information that is technological in nature, which under Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(a)(4) requires that the process of experimentation fundamentally rely on principles of the physical or biological sciences, engineering, or computer science.

Business Component Test (§ 41(d)(1)(B)(ii)): The taxpayer must intend that the information to be discovered be useful in the development of a new or improved business component (defined in § 41(d)(2)(B) as any product, process, computer software, technique, formula, or invention which is to be held for sale, lease, or license, or used by the taxpayer in a trade or business of the taxpayer).

Process of Experimentation Test (§ 41(d)(1)(C)): Substantially all (defined in Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(a)(6) as 80 percent or more, measured on a cost or another consistently applied reasonable basis) of the research activities must constitute elements of a process of experimentation that relates to a qualified purpose under § 41(d)(3)(A)—namely, a new or improved function, performance, or reliability or quality of the business component.

body.text: The controlling statutory and regulatory language in Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(a)(4) refers more broadly to principles of the "physical or biological sciences, engineering, or computer science." Thus, physical sciences such as chemistry, materials science, metallurgy, geology, and thermodynamics are fully encompassed within the statutory scope, whereas "physics" and "biology" alone state the rule too narrowly.

Under Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(a)(5)(i), a process of experimentation is a process designed to evaluate one or more alternatives to achieve a result where the capability or the method of achieving that result, or the appropriate design of that result, is uncertain as of the beginning of the taxpayer's research activities. This regulatory standard requires that the taxpayer identify the uncertainty regarding the development or improvement of a business component, identify one or more alternatives intended to eliminate that uncertainty, and identify and conduct a process of evaluating those alternatives (through modeling, simulation, or a systematic trial and error methodology). Costs incurred where the capability, method, and appropriate design are already readily discernible and known to skilled professionals at the outset do not satisfy Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(a)(5) and are excluded.
3. Statutory exclusions under IRC § 41(d)(4) and related rules
3.1 Research after commercial production

IRC § 41(d)(4)(A) expressly excludes any research conducted after the beginning of commercial production of the business component. Under Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(c)(2)(i), activities are treated as conducted after the beginning of commercial production if they are conducted after the business component is developed to the point where it is ready for commercial sale or use, or meets the basic functional and economic requirements of the taxpayer for the component's sale or use.

Furthermore, Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(c)(2)(ii) establishes a bright-line per se list of activities that are conclusively deemed to occur after the beginning of commercial production and are therefore excluded from qualified research:

items: Preproduction planning for a finished business component;
Tooling-up for production;
Trial production runs;
Troubleshooting involving the detection of faults in production equipment or processes;
Accumulating data relating to production processes; and
Debugging flaws in a business component.

body.text: Specifically, Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(c)(2)(iii) provides that in cases involving development of both a product and a manufacturing or other commercial production process for the product, the commercial-production exclusion applies separately to the product and the process. Under the "shrinking-back rule" of Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(b)(2) and the separate-business-component rule of § 1.41-4(c)(2)(iii), once a chemical formula or pharmaceutical compound is synthesized at laboratory scale, the development of the commercial-scale manufacturing process is evaluated as a separate business component; its costs qualify if and only if scaling up the production process independently presents technological uncertainty regarding capability, method, or process design and undergoes its own systematic process of experimentation prior to the commercial readiness of that manufacturing process. Moreover, Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(c)(2)(iv) explicitly provides that clinical investigation of a pharmaceutical product is not treated as occurring after commercial production solely because the product is commercially available for other indications, whereas post-marketing clinical trials (such as Phase IV drug surveillance studies that do not seek FDA approval for new therapeutic indications or formulations) are generally excluded unless they establish new functional or therapeutic parameters through experimentation.
3.2 Routine testing, quality control, surveys, and data collection

items: Efficiency surveys;
Activity relating to management functions or techniques;
Market research, testing, or development (including advertising or promotions);
Routine data collection; or
Routine or ordinary testing or inspection for quality control.

body.text: Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(c)(5) reinforces this statutory bar verbatim. Crucially, the regulation distinguishes between excluded routine quality-control testing—which merely verifies that a product or batch conforms to established specifications—and validation testing conducted as part of a systematic process of experimentation prior to commercial production to eliminate design or methodological uncertainty.

The National Science Foundation (NSF) National Center for Science and Engineering Statistics (NCSES) compilation of official R&D definitions confirms that the Business Enterprise Research and Development (BERD) Survey definition likewise excludes routine product testing, quality control, and technical services unless they are an integral part of an active R&D project, and excludes market research, efficiency surveys, and management studies.

In United States federal tax law, IRC § 41(d)(4)(D) and Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(c)(5)(iii) explicitly exclude "market research, testing, or development (including advertising or promotions)." By contrast, the statistical NSF BERD survey definition focuses on market research and management studies without specifically enumerating public relations or advertising; for federal income tax compliance, IRC § 41(d)(4)(D) is the controlling legal authority.
3.3 Non-technological research: social sciences, arts, humanities, and cosmetic design
Two interlocking subsections of IRC § 41 exclude non-technological and aesthetic activities:

items: Social Sciences, Arts, and Humanities (§ 41(d)(4)(G)): IRC § 41(d)(4)(G) and Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(c)(8) categorically exclude any research in the social sciences (including economics, business management, and behavioral sciences), arts, or humanities.

Style, Taste, Cosmetic, or Seasonal Design Factors (§ 41(d)(3)(B)): IRC § 41(d)(3)(B) provides that research shall not be treated as conducted for a qualified purpose if it relates to style, taste, cosmetic, or seasonal design factors.

body.text: The NSF BERD Survey definition expressly excludes literary, artistic, or historical projects, such as films, music, or books and other publications. The literal phrasing referencing films, music, or books originates in the NSF BERD survey instructions; in United States tax law, the corresponding legal exclusion is phrased more broadly in IRC § 41(d)(4)(G) and Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(c)(8) as "research in the social sciences, arts, or humanities," supplemented by the disallowed-purpose rule in IRC § 41(d)(3)(B) for style, taste, cosmetic, or seasonal design factors.
3.4 Adaptation and duplication (reverse engineering)

IRC § 41(d)(4)(B) and Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(c)(3) exclude any activities relating to adapting an existing business component to a particular customer's requirement or need. If the development of a custom component for a specific customer requires resolving fundamental technological uncertainty regarding capability, method, or design through a process of experimentation under § 41(d)(1), the activity is not barred by the adaptation exclusion. Conversely, modifying an existing product's dimensions, interfaces, or configuration parameters using known engineering methods to fit a customer's site specifications is excluded under § 41(d)(4)(B).

IRC § 41(d)(4)(C) and Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(c)(4) exclude any activity relating to the reproduction of an existing business component (in whole or in part) from a physical examination of the business component itself or from plans, blueprints, detailed specifications, or publicly available information with respect to such business component. While this rule categorically excludes reverse engineering and duplication costs, Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(c)(4) specifies that merely examining a competitor's existing business component in the course of developing the taxpayer's own distinct component that otherwise satisfies IRC § 41(d)(1) does not by itself trigger the duplication exclusion.

Technical Analysis: Under Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(c)(3) and the internal-use software rules of Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(c)(6), routine configuration, parameterization, data migration, and integration of commercial off-the-shelf (COTS) software using standard vendor APIs are excluded because they adapt existing functionality without resolving technological uncertainty through experimentation.
3.5 Administrative overhead and indirect costs
Under United States tax law, the controlling exclusionary rules are codified in IRC § 41(b)(2) and detailed in Treas. Reg. § 1.41-2:

items: Direct Supervision Limitation (Treas. Reg. § 1.41-2(c)(2)): Under IRC § 41(b)(2)(B)(ii), only wages paid for "qualified services"—engaging in, directly supervising, or directly supporting qualified research—are eligible. Treas. Reg. § 1.41-2(c)(2) defines "direct supervision" strictly as the immediate supervision (first-line management) of qualified research (for example, a research scientist who directly supervises laboratory experiments even if not personally performing the physical experiments). Direct supervision explicitly excludes supervision by a higher-level manager (second-tier or "two-up" management and above) to whom first-line managers report, even if that higher-level manager is a qualified research scientist or chief technology officer.

Direct Support vs. General and Administrative Services (Treas. Reg. § 1.41-2(c)(3)): "Direct support" encompasses services in the direct support of persons either engaging in the actual conduct of qualified research or directly supervising such persons (for example, a machinist machining a part for an experimental model, a laboratory worker cleaning equipment used in qualified research, a clerk compiling research test data, or a secretary typing reports describing laboratory results). However, Treas. Reg. § 1.41-2(c)(3)(ii) explicitly excludes general and administrative (G&A) services and other services that only indirectly benefit research activities, regardless of whether those administrative personnel are assigned to the R&D department or a separate corporate department. The regulation specifically lists payroll personnel preparing salary checks of laboratory scientists, accountants accounting for research expenses, janitors performing general cleaning of a research laboratory, and corporate officers engaged in supervising financial or personnel (HR) matters as excluded.

Exclusion of Non-Taxable Fringe Benefits and Non-W-2 Compensation (IRC § 41(b)(2)(D) & Treas. Reg. § 1.41-2(d)(1)): Under IRC § 41(b)(2)(D)(i), "wages" for R&D credit purposes have the meaning given by IRC § 3401(a) (federal income tax withholding wages, generally reported in Box 1 of Form W-2). Consequently, non-taxable employee fringe benefits, employer matching contributions to 401(k) or qualified pension plans, employer-paid health insurance premiums, employer portions of FICA/FUTA payroll taxes, and wages used in computing the Work Opportunity Tax Credit under IRC § 51 (§ 41(b)(2)(D)(iii)) are strictly excluded from QREs.

Exclusion of Indirect Supplies and General Overhead (Treas. Reg. § 1.41-2(b)(1)–(2)): Under Treas. Reg. § 1.41-2(b)(1), expenditures for supplies or for the use of personal property that represent indirect research expenditures or general and administrative expenses do not qualify as in-house research expenses. Under Treas. Reg. § 1.41-2(b)(2), general utility expenditures (such as standard electricity, water, gas, telephone, and internet service for a building in which research is performed) are excluded as G&A overhead, subject only to a narrow regulatory exception where the taxpayer can establish that the special character of the qualified research required extraordinary additional utility expenditures (for example, operating a high-energy wind tunnel or cryogenic chamber).

body.text: Regulatory Distinction Noted: For United States tax compliance, however, statistical survey definitions have zero legal force; IRC § 41(b) and Treas. Reg. § 1.41-2 strictly prohibit the inclusion of indirect overhead, facilities maintenance, rent, and G&A expenses in the QRE calculation.
3.6 Funded research and substantial rights

IRC § 41(d)(4)(H) excludes any research to the extent funded by any grant, contract, or otherwise by another person (or any governmental entity). The implementing rules in Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4A(d) establish a two-prong test—commonly analyzed in federal jurisprudence (such as Fairchild Industries, Inc. v. United States, 71 F.3d 868 (Fed. Cir. 1995), Lockheed Martin Corp. v. United States, 210 F.3d 1366 (Fed. Cir. 2000), and Geosyntec Consultants, Inc. v. United States, 776 F.3d 1330 (11th Cir. 2015)) as the economic risk (contingency of payment) requirement and the substantial rights requirement:

items: Economic Risk / Contingency of Payment (Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4A(d)(1)): In determining whether research is funded, all agreements (not only research contracts) entered into between the taxpayer performing the research and the customer or sponsor are examined. Amounts payable under any agreement that are contingent on the success of the research (meaning payment is owed only if the research successfully produces the required technical result or deliverable meeting acceptance testing) are treated as paid for the product or result of the research and are not treated as funding. Conversely, if the researcher is entitled to payment regardless of whether the research succeeds (such as under a standard cost-plus or non-contingent time-and-materials contract where the customer bears the financial risk of failure), the research is treated as funded and the researcher's expenditures are excluded.

Retention of Substantial Rights (Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4A(d)(2)): If a taxpayer performing research for another person retains no substantial rights in the research under the agreement providing for the research, the research is treated as fully funded under § 41(d)(4)(H), and none of the taxpayer's expenditures in performing it are allowed as QREs—even if payment was contingent on success. Under § 1.41-4A(d)(2), a taxpayer does not retain substantial rights if the customer retains exclusive rights to the research results or if the taxpayer must pay a royalty or fee to the customer to use the results of the research in the taxpayer's own future business. Incidental benefits (such as generic workforce experience or skill retention) do not constitute substantial rights.

Pro-Rata Partial Funding Rule (Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4A(d)(3)): Where a taxpayer retains substantial rights in the research, but the research is partially funded through non-contingent payments that are less than the total cost of the research, the research is excluded only to the extent of the funded portion; the unfunded excess expenditures borne at the taxpayer's own risk remain potentially eligible.

body.text: Technical Analysis: Furthermore, when the customer (payor) claims contract research expenses under IRC § 41(b)(3) and Treas. Reg. § 1.41-2(e), the reverse mirror of the funding rule applies: the contract research agreement must be (i) entered into prior to the performance of the qualified research, (ii) provide that the research be performed on behalf of the taxpayer, and (iii) require the taxpayer to bear the expense even if the research is not successful (Treas. Reg. § 1.41-2(e)(2)). Even when all three conditions are met, IRC § 41(b)(3)(A) automatically excludes 35 percent of the contract research expenditure by limiting the statutory inclusion to 65 percent of the amounts paid or incurred (or 75 percent for payments to qualified research consortia under § 41(b)(3)(C), and 100 percent for eligible small businesses, universities, or federal laboratories under the energy research provisions of § 41(b)(3)(D)). Additionally, under IRC § 41(b)(3)(B), any prepaid contract research expense attributable to research to be conducted after the close of the taxable year is excluded from the current year's QREs and deferred until the taxable year in which the qualified research is actually conducted.
3.7 Research conducted outside the United States
IRC § 41(d)(4)(F) and Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(c)(7) categorically exclude any research conducted outside the United States, the Commonwealth of Puerto Rico, or any possession of the United States.

Under IRC § 41(d)(4)(F) and Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(c)(7), the exclusion is not limited to projects conducted "entirely" outside the country; rather, the geographic exclusion applies on an activity-by-activity and expenditure-by-expenditure basis. If a domestic research project includes segments performed by employees or independent contractors physically located outside the United States, the Commonwealth of Puerto Rico, or a U.S. possession, the specific wages, supplies, or contract research costs attributable to the work physically performed outside those jurisdictions are strictly excluded from QREs, even if the overall project is directed from the United States and the resulting intellectual property is owned by a U.S. corporation. Conversely, research physically conducted within the Commonwealth of Puerto Rico or any U.S. possession (such as Guam, the U.S. Virgin Islands, American Samoa, or the Commonwealth of the Northern Mariana Islands) is expressly inside the permitted statutory territory under § 41(d)(4)(F).

In United States federal tax law, IRC § 41 contains no stand-alone statutory exclusion barring domestic research merely because it is performed for a foreign customer or foreign affiliate. Rather, domestic research performed in the United States for a foreign party is governed by the standard funded-research rules of IRC § 41(d)(4)(H) and Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4A(d) (and, for controlled groups, the single-taxpayer aggregation rules of IRC § 41(f)(1) and Treas. Reg. § 1.41-6). If a U.S. taxpayer performs research in the United States under contract for an unrelated foreign entity that pays on a non-contingent basis or retains exclusive rights, the expenses are excluded under the funded-research bar of § 41(d)(4)(H), not under a separate foreign-beneficiary exclusion.
3.8 Capital items, depreciable property, and internal-use software exclusions
Specifically, IRC § 41(b)(2)(C) defines "supplies" as any tangible property other than:

items: Land or improvements to land (§ 41(b)(2)(C)(i)); and
Property of a character subject to the allowance for depreciation (§ 41(b)(2)(C)(ii)).

body.text: Under Treas. Reg. § 1.41-2(b)(1), property is considered to be of a character subject to the allowance for depreciation (and therefore excluded from QREs) if it is depreciable in the hands of the taxpayer under IRC § 167 or § 168, even if the taxpayer elects to expense the asset immediately under IRC § 179 or claims bonus depreciation under IRC § 168(k). Furthermore, the annual depreciation allowance or amortization deduction itself is expressly barred from being treated as a qualified research expenditure under both IRC § 41(b)(2)(C)(ii) and IRC § 174A(c).

In addition to tangible capital assets, IRC § 41(d)(4)(E) and Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(c)(6) establish a specific statutory exclusion for internal-use software (IUS). Except to the extent provided in Treasury regulations, computer software developed by (or for the benefit of) the taxpayer primarily for internal use by the taxpayer in general and administrative functions (specifically financial management, human resources management, and support services functions under Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(c)(6)(iii)) is excluded from qualified research unless it satisfies either a statutory exception (such as software developed as part of a hardware-software package or used directly in an activity that itself constitutes qualified research) or the stringent three-part "High Threshold of Innovation" test under Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(c)(6)(vii):

items: Innovative (§ 1.41-4(c)(6)(vii)(B)): The software is intended to be unique or novel and to differ in a significant and inventive way from prior software implementations or methods, such that it would result in a reduction in cost or improvement in speed or other measurable operating improvement that is substantial and economically significant;

Significant Economic Risk (§ 1.41-4(c)(6)(vii)(C)): The software development involves significant economic risk, meaning the taxpayer commits substantial resources to the development and there is substantial uncertainty, because of technical risk, that such resources would be recovered within a reasonable period; and

Not Commercially Available (§ 1.41-4(c)(6)(vii)(D)): The software is not commercially available for use by the taxpayer in that it cannot be purchased, leased, or licensed and used for the intended purpose without modifications that would satisfy the innovation and significant economic risk requirements.

body.text: 4. United Kingdom: overseas restrictions and externally provided workers

HMRC guidance (draft guidance updated March 27, 2024, enacted via the Finance Act 2024 and reflected in HMRC's Corporate Intangibles Research and Development Manual) confirms that the statutory restrictions on overseas contracted-out R&D and overseas EPWs apply to accounting periods beginning on or after April 1, 2024, coinciding with the introduction of the merged Research and Development Expenditure Credit (RDEC) scheme and the Enhanced R&D Intensive Support (ERIS) regime.

For EPWs, HMRC applies the Pay As You Earn (PAYE) and Class 1 National Insurance Contributions (NIC) requirement as a mandatory statutory gateway: EPW earnings qualify only if the claimant company or the staff provider/controller is required to operate UK PAYE and account for Class 1 NIC on those earnings (wholly or in part), unless the expenditure satisfies the narrow statutory exemption for qualifying overseas R&D under Corporation Tax Act 2009 (CTA 2009) section 1138A (HMRC manual CIRD137000).

For payments made to an unconnected staff provider, CTA 2009 and CIRD137000 limit the claimable expenditure to 65 percent of the payment attributable to qualifying EPW earnings (automatically excluding the remaining 35 percent markup element). Connected parties may jointly elect in writing, irrevocably and within two years after the end of the relevant accounting period, to be treated as connected so that the lower of the actual staff provision cost and the payment made can be claimed without the arbitrary 65 percent cap.

Assuming equal remuneration across all ten workers, 60 percent of the total payment to the staff provider is attributable to qualifying UK EPW earnings, and the 40 percent share attributable to the four overseas workers in Mexico is excluded at the gateway. Under the statutory rule in CTA 2009 and CIRD137000 for unconnected staff providers, the 65 percent unconnected-EPW restriction applies on top of that 60 percent qualifying share, meaning that only 39 percent (60% multiplied by 65%) of the total invoice paid to the unconnected staff provider is potentially eligible (with 61 percent excluded overall).

Additional statutory nuance (CTA 2009 s 1138A overseas exception): Overseas R&D costs remain eligible in the UK only where three cumulative conditions under CTA 2009 s 1138A are satisfied: (1) geographical, environmental, or social conditions necessary for the R&D are not present in the UK; (2) those conditions are present in the overseas location where the R&D is undertaken; and (3) it would be wholly unreasonable for the company to replicate those conditions in the UK (or where specific legal or regulatory requirements mandate that the activities take place outside the UK). CTA 2009 s 1138A expressly excludes cost of work and availability of workers as valid grounds for claiming overseas R&D expenditure.
4.1 Worked example (hypothetical)

cells: Total payment to unconnected staff provider for 10 workers
Excluded share for 4 remote workers in Mexico (not on UK PAYE/NIC)
Share attributable to 6 UK workers on PAYE/NIC (equal wages)
Potentially eligible expenditure as % of total payment

body.text: Note: Further pro-rata exclusion applies if the six UK workers are only partially engaged in qualifying R&D activities during the accounting period.
4.2 Capital allowances are a separate relief

In the United Kingdom, capital expenditure is excluded from revenue R&D tax relief schemes (merged RDEC and ERIS) and is instead relieved through the capital allowances regime, including the Annual Investment Allowance (AIA), which provides a permanent 100 percent first-year allowance on the first £1 million of qualifying plant and machinery expenditure, alongside 100 percent Research and Development Allowances (RDAs) under Part 6 of the Capital Allowances Act 2001 for capital assets (excluding land) used for R&D. This parallels the United States rule in IRC § 41(b)(2)(C), which excludes depreciable property and land from R&D tax credit supplies and routes capital equipment recovery through IRC §§ 167, 168, and 179.
5. Australia: capital, core technology, and nexus exclusions

items: Lack of Direct and Close Connection: Under Division 355 of the ITAA 1997, a notional R&D deduction is unavailable for overhead or operating expenses that lack the requisite nexus ("incurred on one or more R&D activities") to registered core or supporting R&D activities. General corporate overhead, executive administration, and marketing expenditures that would be incurred regardless of the R&D activities are excluded.

Building Acquisition and Construction (ITAA 1997 s 355-225(1)(a)): Expenditure incurred to acquire or construct a building (or part of a building) or an extension, alteration, or improvement to a building is statutorily ineligible for the R&D tax incentive. Such structural expenditures may instead be eligible for standard capital works deductions under Division 43 of the ITAA 1997.

Tangible Depreciating Assets (ITAA 1997 s 355-225(1)(b)): The capital acquisition cost of a tangible depreciating asset is excluded from notional R&D expenditure deductions; instead, only the notional decline in value (depreciation) during the period the asset is used for R&D activities is addressed under the separate R&D decline-in-value provisions of Subdivision 355-E.

Core Technology Expenditure (ITAA 1997 s 355-225(1)(d)): Expenditure incurred in acquiring technology (or the right to use technology) that constitutes "core technology" is excluded from the R&D tax incentive. Under s 355-225(2), technology is core technology for R&D activities if the purpose of the R&D activities was or is to obtain new knowledge based on that technology, or to create new or improved materials, products, devices, processes, or services to be based on that technology. Taxpayers uncertain whether acquired technology constitutes core technology may request a formal finding from the Department of Industry, Science and Resources (DISR).

Additional Statutory Exclusions under ITAA 1997 s 355-225 and s 355-405: Section 355-225(1)(c) also explicitly excludes interest expenditure (and amounts in the nature of interest) within the meaning of Division 16G of Part III of the ITAA 1936, while s 355-405 excludes expenditure that is not "at risk" (mirroring the economic-risk principle of IRC § 41(d)(4)(H) in the United States). Additionally, salary expenditure incurred in constructing a tangible depreciating asset or a building is excluded from direct R&D notional deductions under s 355-225.

body.text: Technical Analysis: Under ITAA 1997 s 355-225(2), the statutory exclusion is specifically targeted at the acquisition or licensing cost of the underlying technology upon which the R&D project is based, whereas subsequent internal R&D expenditures incurred by the taxpayer to further develop or build upon that technology remain potentially eligible. In the United States, the acquisition or licensing of existing patents or third-party intellectual property is similarly excluded from IRC § 41 QREs because patents and licenses are intangible assets—falling completely outside the IRC § 41(b)(2)(C) definition of "supplies" (which requires non-depreciable tangible property)—and are expressly barred under Treas. Reg. § 1.174-2(a)(4), which excludes the acquisition of another's patent, model, production, or process from research or experimental expenditures.
6.1 Expatriate relocation costs and non-wage employee benefits

Under United States federal tax law, the treatment of employee relocation reimbursements, moving allowances, housing stipends, and tuition benefits is governed directly by IRC § 41(b)(2)(B), IRC § 41(b)(2)(D), and Treas. Reg. § 1.41-2(d)(1):

items: Even where moving expense reimbursements or housing stipends are includible in an employee's taxable Form W-2 Box 1 wages (noting that the IRC § 132(g) exclusion for qualified moving expense reimbursements is suspended for non-military taxpayers and permanently repealed for non-armed-forces/intelligence employees under Pub. L. 119-21), IRC § 41(b)(2)(B) and Treas. Reg. § 1.41-2(d)(1) mandate that wages constitute in-house research expenses only to the extent they are paid or incurred for "qualified services" performed by the employee (engaging in, directly supervising, or directly supporting qualified research).

Reimbursements for relocating an employee's household, temporary living allowances, and dependent school tuition are administrative recruitment or relocation outlays, not remuneration for the time spent performing qualified research services; when properly segregated from compensation for qualified services, or to the extent they represent non-taxable fringe benefits excluded from IRC § 3401(a) wages, they cannot be used to inflate QREs without proper allocation under Treas. Reg. § 1.41-2(d)(1).

body.text: 6.2 NIH acquisition-cost definition and GAAP software capitalization rules

In United States R&D tax credit audits, this distinction is governed directly by IRC § 41(b)(2)(C) and Treas. Reg. § 1.41-2(b)(1), as interpreted in federal case law (including Lockheed Martin Corp. v. United States, 210 F.3d 1366 (Fed. Cir. 2000), and TG Missouri Corp. v. Commissioner, 133 T.C. 278 (2009)). Any capital equipment together with the ancillary modifications, attachments, freight, and installation costs capitalized into the depreciable basis of that equipment under IRC §§ 263(a) and 167 is excluded from QREs as "property of a character subject to the allowance for depreciation" under IRC § 41(b)(2)(C)(ii). Only non-depreciable tangible materials and prototype components consumed or destroyed in the testing and experimentation process qualify as "supplies" under § 41(b)(2)(A)(ii).
7. High-risk "gray zone" allocations and IRS audit substantiation standards

items: Mixed-Use Labor and the "Substantially All" Rule:

Under IRC § 41(b)(2)(B) and Treas. Reg. § 1.41-2(d)(1), if an employee performs both qualified services and non-qualified services (such as routine maintenance, customer technical support, sales engineering, or general administration), only the amount of wages allocable to the qualified services may be included in QREs. Under Treas. Reg. § 1.41-2(d)(1), in the absence of another method that the taxpayer can establish is more reasonable, this allocation is determined by multiplying the employee's total taxable wages by the ratio of total time actually spent performing qualified services to total time spent performing all services for the employer. Only if "substantially all" of an employee's services during the taxable year consist of qualified services—defined strictly in Treas. Reg. § 1.41-2(d)(2) as at least 80 percent of the employee's wages/time—may 100 percent of that employee's wages be included. Federal courts (such as in United States v. McFerrin, 570 F.3d 672 (5th Cir. 2009), Shami v. Commissioner, 741 F.3d 560 (5th Cir. 2014), and Siemer Milling Co. v. Commissioner, T.C. Memo. 2019-37) consistently disallow unsubstantiated oral estimates where taxpayers fail to provide credible nexus linking employee wages to qualified research activities at the business-component level.
Post-Launch Testing, Debugging, and Maintenance:

Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(c)(2)(ii) conclusively deems "debugging flaws in a business component" and "troubleshooting that involves detecting faults in production equipment or processes" to occur after the beginning of commercial production under IRC § 41(d)(4)(A), barring their inclusion in QREs.
IRS Examination Enforcement, Form 6765 Section G, and Chief Counsel Refund-Claim Requirements:

IRS Form 6765 (Credit for Increasing Research Activities) Business Component Reporting: Beginning with the revised Form 6765 (Section G, Business Component Information), the IRS requires taxpayers (subject to specified small-business and QRE-threshold exceptions) to report granular, business-component-by-business-component QRE breakdowns on the return itself, segregating direct research wages, direct supervision wages, direct support wages, supplies, computer rental, and contract research by each specific business component.

IRS Chief Counsel Memorandum 20214101F (Refund Claim Specificity under Treas. Reg. § 301.6402-2(b)(1)): For amended returns claiming an R&D credit refund, the IRS requires taxpayers to identify at the time of filing: (1) all business components to which the IRC § 41 research credit claim relates for that year, (2) for each business component, all research activities performed, and (3) the total qualified employee wage expenses, total qualified supply expenses, and total qualified contract research expenses for the claim year. Failure to segregate excluded expenses at the business-component level can render an amended refund claim legally deficient or trigger the 20 percent accuracy-related penalty under IRC § 6662(a) or the erroneous claim for refund or credit penalty (20 percent of the excessive amount) under IRC § 6676.

8.1 Fee structure and Circular 230 contingent fee restrictions

In United States tax practice, contingent fee arrangements are strictly regulated by Treasury Department Circular No. 230 (31 C.F.R. § 10.27). Under 31 C.F.R. § 10.27(b)(1), a practitioner (including CPAs, attorneys, and Enrolled Agents practicing before the IRS) is generally prohibited from charging a contingent fee for services rendered in connection with any matter before the Internal Revenue Service, including preparing or filing an original tax return. Moreover, AICPA Code of Professional Conduct Rule 1.510.001 bars CPAs from charging contingent fees for preparing original or amended tax returns or claims for a tax refund unless specific narrow regulatory exceptions apply. Avoiding percentage-based contingency fees aligns directly with the ethical standards of Circular 230 and reduces audit risk associated with aggressive QRE inflation.
8.3 ISO 31000 risk management

items: Non-Certifiable Guidance Standard: According to ISO's official specification for ISO 31000 (Risk management — Guidelines), ISO 31000 provides principles and guidelines for managing risk and cannot be used for certification purposes (unlike management system standards that contain "Requirements," such as ISO/IEC 27001 or ISO 9001). An organization can align its internal risk management framework with ISO 31000 guidelines, but no accredited body can issue an "ISO 31000 certification."
Superseded Edition: ISO 31000:2018 (Second Edition, published in February 2018) officially cancelled and replaced the first edition (ISO 31000:2009).

body.text: 8.4 Six-Eye Review and TaxTrex software screening

items: Six-Eye Review: Every R&D tax credit claim undergoes sequential review by three separate specialists before submission: (i) a qualified engineer or scientist who evaluates technical project eligibility against the IRC § 41(d)(1) Four-Part Test; (ii) a certified public accountant (CPA) or Enrolled Agent (EA) who audits the financial ledger, wage allocations, and statutory exclusions under IRC § 41(b) and § 41(d)(4); and (iii) a senior quality-control principal who performs a final compliance review.

TaxTrex Software Platform: The firm's proprietary R&D tax software requires users to map specific labor and supply line items directly to documented technical uncertainties and processes of experimentation at the business-component level, flagging unlinked or administrative cost items for exclusion in alignment with IRS Form 6765 Section G substantiation standards.

cells: Research conducted after the beginning of commercial production (including preproduction planning, tooling-up, trial production runs, production troubleshooting, data accumulation, and debugging flaws); adaptation of an existing business component to a specific customer's requirement; duplication or reverse engineering from physical examination, plans, blueprints, or specs; efficiency surveys, management functions/studies, market research, advertising/promotions, routine data collection, and routine QC testing; internal-use software (unless meeting the High Threshold of Innovation test or an exception); foreign research conducted outside the U.S., Puerto Rico, or U.S. possessions; research in the social sciences, arts, or humanities; research relating to style, taste, cosmetic, or seasonal design factors; and funded research where payment is not contingent on success or the taxpayer retains no substantial rights.

Higher-level ("two-up" or executive) management wages beyond immediate first-line supervision; general and administrative (G&A) support wages (HR, payroll, accounting, janitorial, corporate officers); non-taxable employee fringe benefits, 401(k)/pension contributions, health insurance premiums, employer payroll taxes, and IRC § 51 WOTC wages; land or improvements to land; property of a character subject to the allowance for depreciation (capital equipment, buildings, and depreciation deductions); intangible asset/patent acquisition costs; general building utilities and overhead; 35% of standard contract research expenses (limiting inclusion to 65%); and prepaid contract research expenses prior to the year research is performed.

Overseas contracted-out R&D and overseas externally provided worker (EPW) costs for accounting periods beginning on or after April 1, 2024 (unless meeting the strict geographical/environmental/regulatory exception under CTA 2009 s 1138A where UK replication is wholly unreasonable); EPW earnings not subject to UK PAYE and Class 1 NIC; 35% of unconnected EPW payments (limiting eligible share to 65%); and capital expenditure (relieved separately via AIA or RDAs).
